clue.text: Conservative and liberal creep in embrace

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal
to inch is to creep forward slowly

explanation.surface: Two rival parties shuffle towards each other in an awkward political hug.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface makes 'Conservative and liberal' look like a coalition; they are just two letters, and 'creep' is a verb, not a sneaky person.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinch is an embrace, as between lovers or boxers holding on.

clue.text: Wind up Tory with hint about dire leader

parts.note: Con is short for Conservative, i.e. a Tory

indicators.note: the leader of 'dire' is its first letter

parts.note: a clue is a hint
first letter of 'dire'

explanation.surface: Someone goads a Conservative by hinting at an awful party leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' reads as 'tease' in the surface, the natural thing to do to a Tory, but the definition means 'finish'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to wind up a meeting or speech is to bring it to a close.

clue.text: I love pasty-looking chap in a state, perhaps

parts.note: used as is
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
wan means pale, pasty-looking

explanation.surface: Someone declares affection for a pale man who is clearly upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' suggests agitation; here it is literal, a man from a US state. 'Perhaps' marks Iowa as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An Iowan is a native of Iowa, one of the US states.

clue.text: Perfume manufacturer getting in new groove?

parts.note: Chanel, maker of No 5
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A fragrance house is trying to find its fresh rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groove' in the surface sounds like getting into the swing of things; it is a physical furrow. N goes after CHAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A channel is a groove or furrow cut into a surface.

clue.text: Alpha female snorts coke of high quality

parts.note: the top lass is the alpha female
C is slang for cocaine

explanation.surface: A domineering woman takes cocaine, and only the best stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has 'of high quality' describing the coke; it is the definition, and 'Alpha female' is a single idea, not two.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something of high quality is first-rate, top of its class.

clue.text: Old worker snarfing seconds could be thus

definitions.text: Old worker snarfing seconds could be thus

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: to snarf is to wolf food down

parts.note: a worker is a worker bee
S is the standard abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: An elderly employee always going back for second helpings might end up this way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: someone wolfing down second helpings could well become obese. S goes inside BEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who keeps eating second helpings could become obese, which is what 'thus' points to.

clue.text: Policeman injecting horse will get the axe

parts.note: a copper is a policeman
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: A police officer shooting up heroin is going to be sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get the axe' reads as being fired; the definition is the axe itself. Horse is drug slang for heroin, and H is heroin's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A chopper is an axe or cleaver, something that chops.

clue.text: No one fart about when Hoskins gets up!

indicators.note: the letters are moved about into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A plea for decorum in the bedroom when the setter finally rises.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a self-deprecating joke by the setter, Hoskins, claiming to lie in until the afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter jokingly claims not to rise until the afternoon.

clue.text: Overindulges and goes off booty

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to spoil a child is to overindulge them
second meaning: of food, to rot or turn bad
third meaning: plunder taken by the victors in war

explanation.surface: Someone who gorges themselves ends up sick, then runs off with the loot.
explanation.walkthrough: Three separate meanings of one word, two verbs and a noun; 'and' only joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The one word covers pampering a child, food decaying, and plunder taken by victors in war.

clue.text: Unusual to grab head of lizard and choke

parts.note: strange means unusual

indicators.note: the head of 'lizard' is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of 'lizard'

explanation.surface: An odd scene: someone seizes a lizard by the head and throttles it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grab' and 'choke' make the surface a single violent act, which hides that 'to grab' is only an instruction to hold a letter inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to choke someone is to throttle them by the neck.

clue.text: Modern fortified building in English city

parts.note: new means modern
a castle is a fortified building

explanation.surface: A recently built fortress stands somewhere in England.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is almost a literal history: Newcastle upon Tyne is named after the 'new castle' built there in 1080.
explanation.definitionFit: Newcastle upon Tyne is a city in north-east England.

clue.text: Best party, getting gone in the head!

parts.note: gone and out both mean away or departed
a do is a party

explanation.surface: The finest party is the one where everyone gets out of their heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like an adjective praising the party; it is a verb, to beat. 'Gone in the head' suggests drunkenness, but just puts OUT first.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to best a rival is to beat or surpass them.

clue.text: Story with knight stealing new bedding?

parts.note: a lie is a made-up story
N is the chess notation for knight
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A tale of a knight who makes off with fresh sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: Two N's with different jobs: the knight is added to the story, and the new one is taken inside. The question mark flags that linen covers more than bedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Bed linen is bedding; the question mark admits linen is also table linen and cloth.

clue.text: A vocal on Substitute or Out of Time?

parts.note: used as is
a temp is a substitute worker
oral and vocal both mean spoken

explanation.surface: A music quiz: is that singing on the Who's Substitute or the Stones' Out of Time?
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make both phrases song titles: Substitute by the Who and Out of Time by the Rolling Stones. Neither is a song here.
explanation.definitionFit: Atemporal means existing outside time, out of time.

clue.text: Unfeeling member very posh girl rejected

parts.note: dead means very, as in 'dead easy'
gel is the posh pronunciation of girl

explanation.surface: A heartless club member turns down a very upper-class young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfeeling member' reads as a cold person in a club; it is a numb limb. A dead leg is a thigh numbed by a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead leg is a leg, a member or limb, left numb and without feeling.

clue.text: It's a crime to break peaceful agreement

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Breaking a peace treaty would be criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a moral statement about treaties, with the anagram fodder disguised as the start of a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a truce, like the agreement that ended fighting on 11 November 1918.

clue.text: French main? Opening unopened wine!

parts.note: the main is the sea, which is mer in French
an opening is a SLOT; without its first letter, LOT

explanation.surface: A French main course, and a bottle of wine left uncorked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like a main course; it is the old word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Merlot is one red grape variety and its wine.

clue.text: Thin Frenchman with brilliant speed

parts.note: M is short for Monsieur
ace means brilliant
rate means speed

explanation.surface: A skinny Frenchman who is dazzlingly fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thin' reads as an adjective describing the Frenchman; it is a verb. To macerate is also, less commonly, to make or grow thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Macerate can mean to cause to waste away or grow thin, as well as to soften by soaking.

clue.text: Ring roads close to old-fashioned school

parts.note: by means near, close to
passé means out of date
S is the standard abbreviation for school

explanation.surface: Roads loop round near an outdated school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring roads' looks like an instruction to circle roads; it is the definition. A British ring road circles a town, as a bypass skirts one.
explanation.definitionFit: Bypasses are roads that take traffic round a town, like ring roads.

clue.text: Hoskins is dim prick all the way through!

parts.note: the setter speaking says I'M
pale means dim, faint

explanation.surface: The setter owns up to being a stupid idiot, totally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim prick' reads as an insult the setter aims at himself; 'dim' goes with the wordplay and 'prick' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to pierce right through with a spike.

clue.text: A wine opened by old American gets you excited

parts.note: used as is
red is wine
O is the standard abbreviation for old
US is short for American

explanation.surface: Uncorking a bottle with an elderly American puts you in high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has an old American opening the wine; in the wordplay the wine itself is opened up and the old American goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: excited in the sense of stirred up or roused.

clue.text: Londoner likely to knock Hoskins's head off?

definitions.text: Londoner likely to knock Hoskins's head off?

parts.note: the definition proper: a particular kind of Londoner

parts.words: likely to knock Hoskins's head off?
parts.note: reads as a threat of violence; really it means dropping the H at the front of the setter's name

explanation.surface: A threat from a violent East Ender to beat up the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: The threat of violence is a decoy: a Cockney, a working-class East Londoner, drops the H at the start of words, knocking the head off 'Hoskins'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cockney is an East Londoner, famous for dropping initial aitches.

clue.text: Is it possible that adolescent is a mess?

parts.note: 'can' asks whether it is possible, as in 'Can it be?'
a teen is an adolescent

explanation.surface: A parent wonders whether their teenager can really be this untidy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A mess' reads as untidiness; it is a place where soldiers eat, and a canteen is exactly that.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is a military dining room, which is a canteen.

clue.text: Dodgy bloke, one Edwina worried about?

definitions.meaning: idiom for a rogue or ne'er-do-well
Edwina Currie warned of salmonella in eggs

explanation.surface: Edwina is anxious about a suspicious man.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1988 the British health minister Edwina Currie caused a scandal by saying most British eggs carried salmonella; the question mark flags the topical allusion.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad egg is a rogue, and a literal bad egg was what Edwina Currie worried about.

clue.text: One who legs it if Rob dances badly

indicators.note: the letters are arranged badly, out of order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Someone flees the dance floor when Rob starts his terrible moves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rob' looks like theft to go with 'legs it', but it is just a name supplying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An absconder is someone who runs away, who legs it.

clue.text: Leader of DUP having sex is quaintly comical

indicators.note: the leader of 'DUP' is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of 'DUP'
a roll in the hay is sex

explanation.surface: The head of a Northern Irish party caught in bed is faintly ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader of DUP' tempts a real politician; it only means D. The DUP is Northern Ireland's Democratic Unionist Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Droll means amusing in an odd or quaint way.

clue.text: Sleep for short while with old man in leather

parts.note: a nap is a short sleep
pa is father, one's old man

explanation.surface: Dad dozes off briefly in his leather armchair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container indicator, but it only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nappa is a soft leather made from sheepskin or lambskin.

clue.text: Vacuous police surrounding free festival

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so 'police' keeps only its outer letters
to surround something is to enclose it

parts.note: outer letters of 'police'
to rid is to free

explanation.surface: Brainless police officers ring a festival that costs nothing to attend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free festival' reads as a no-cost event; 'free' is a verb giving RID. RID goes between P and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Pride is the annual LGBTQ+ festival and march.

clue.text: Sinful things produced by out-of-head fiends

indicators.note: DEVILS is out of its head, losing its first letter

parts.note: fiends are DEVILS; the head letter D goes

explanation.surface: Wicked deeds committed by demons who are off their faces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out-of-head' looks like drug slang for high; it means the first letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sins and wrongdoings are evils.

clue.text: Drinking booze? So then sip to get drunk!

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Someone decides the next step is to drink until drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about drinking, and so is the answer: 'on the piss' is British slang for out drinking heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: On the piss is British slang for out on a heavy drinking session.

clue.text: Girl eyed criminal in a rapacious way

indicators.note: the letters are criminally misused, rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A young woman looks over a crook with an acquisitive gleam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' reads as a noun, the thing the girl eyed; it is an adjective signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Greedily means rapaciously, grabbing more than one's share.

clue.text: A northern set with southern backers

parts.note: used as is
N is the standard abbreviation for northern
jelly sets, or gels
S is the standard abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: A group from the North has some supporters from the South.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like a noun, a group; it is a verb. Angels are investors who fund stage shows.
explanation.definitionFit: Angels are financial backers, especially of theatre productions.
